newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN chief confident his reforms will be approved.
newsitem.headline: UN chief confident his reforms will be approved.

text.p: Secretary-General Kofi Annan says he expects the Third World countries to approve his proposed staff cuts, some of whose delegates were miffed on Tuesday about his ongoing dialogue with U.S. Congress members on initial plans to reform the United Nations.

"They will have to approve it, and I am pretty confident they will because of the ground work and preparatory work we have done in moving them along," Annan told Reuters of his 10-point programme revealed on Monday.

The measures were intended to send a signal to Capitol Hill that Annan was ready to undergo serious reform. Sen. Jesse Helms, head of the U.S. Senate Foreign Relations Committee, intends to link the pace to reform to the payment of the huge debt Washington owes the world body, a concept most U.N. members find a high political price to pay.

Annan said he wanted removed from the books the 1,000 posts his predecessor Boutros Boutros-Ghali of Egypt had left vacant through attrition and buy-outs in the core bureaucracies in New York, Geneva, Vienna and Nairobi.
Boutros-Ghali also proposed those jobs be cut. He immediately ran into problems in a General Assembly committee, dominated by developing countries, for wanting to fire 36 people outright.

"If it was rejected it doesn't mean it is not a good thing to go back again. It is really a question of leadership to put it forward and get it accepted. So this is going to be a test," Annan told Reuters.
Western diplomats, particularly Europeans, were enthusiastic about the proposals, many hoping that they would persuade the Congress to pay the money owed.

But other envoys said that several delegations from developing countries felt Annan was catering to rightwing American legislators. Several delegates expressed annoyance that Annan had spoken to Helms as well as House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich before or around the same time he briefed them.
Mark Thiessen, Helms' spokesman, said Annan's programme was a "very small step but it is going in the right direction."
"We want to see the bureaucracy cut, not a shell game," he said on Tuesday. "Only in the surreal world of the United Nations can you eliminate jobs without retiring anyone."
And he added, "Once the heat for reform dies, we want to see those jobs never filled again and that is progress."

Annan, a Ghanaian, said he would trim the new 1998-99 budget by $123 million, somewhat less than his predecessor had once proposed. But he also promised to cut administrative costs by a third over the next few years and use the funds for development programmes.
Another proposal involves recombining three economic and social departments into one, currently costing $122 million and employing about 700 people.
They were split up to give jobs to officials from France and China who had no major posts in New York. The reconstituted department will go to an Indian national.
Under Annan, a French official now heads the peacekeeping department and a Chinese official will get a newly created department for general assembly and conference affairs.
Asked if this was set up to placate China, diplomats and U.N. officials said the new department had been recommended by an efficiency board to stop overlapping functions.
